content: ZW10, also known as Centromere/Kinetochore Protein ZW10 Homolog, is a protein encoded by the ZW10 gene in humans. This protein plays a critical role in ensuring accurate chromosome segregation during cell division. It achieves this by binding to centromeres during the prophase, metaphase, and early anaphase stages of cell division, and to kinetochore microtubules specifically during metaphase. ZW10 was initially identified as a mitotic checkpoint protein essential for chromosome segregation. It is also involved in targeting cytoplasmic dynein and dynactin to mitotic kinetochores. Beyond its role in dividing cells, ZW10 is important in non-dividing cells as well. In these cells, it facilitates the targeting of cytoplasmic dynein to the Golgi apparatus and other membranes, as well as mediating SNARE-dependent trafficking between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and the Golgi. Experimental disruption of ZW10 function, such as through dominant-negative ZW10, anti-ZW10 antibodies, or ZW10 RNA interference (RNAi), leads to the dispersal of the Golgi apparatus. ZW10 RNAi also causes the dispersal of endosomes and lysosomes, further highlighting its role in intracellular trafficking. In Drosophila, kinetochore components such as Rough Deal (Rod) and ZW10 are required for the proper functioning of the metaphase checkpoint. This checkpoint is part of the eukaryotic spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), which monitors the attachment of microtubules to kinetochores and prevents the onset of anaphase until all kinetochores are correctly aligned on the metaphase plate. The SAC is a critical surveillance mechanism that ensures high-fidelity chromosome segregation during mitosis. In higher eukaryotes, cytoplasmic dynein plays a role in silencing the SAC by removing checkpoint proteins, such as Mad2 and the Rod-ZW10-Zwilch complex (RZZ), from aligned kinetochores. This process is essential for the proper progression of mitosis and the maintenance of genomic stability.
